abstract: Light competition drives ecological and evolutionary processes in forests. Real canopies are too complex to simulate in full, so stand models approximate them. We assessed three canopy approximations, the Perfect Plasticity Approximation (PPA), Flat Top and Deep Crown, in two stages. First, we compared their instantaneous light interception with a high-resolution reference model (MAESPA), focusing on competition among individuals and on vulnerability to self-shading. Second, we embedded them in a dynamic vegetation model and traced effects on stand development, demographic equilibrium and invasion fitness, the basis of evolutionary prediction. Deep Crown, which allows leaf area to overlap between individuals, reproduced MAESPA's continuous response of light capture to height. The PPA, and the Flat Top in stands of uniform height, instead produced a stepwise response around the point where a focal tree becomes taller than its neighbours. In the dynamic model, the PPA's discontinuities were tolerable for stand development but shifted demographic equilibrium by an order of magnitude. Every runnable representation produced a continuously stable strategy (CSS), but under the PPA it was reached through a stepped, erratic selection gradient and was not robustly located. All approximations overestimated light capture under self-shading, increasingly so at realistic leaf area. Our results show that continuity of the shade each plant casts as a function of height, rather than average accuracy or assimilation detail, determines whether an approximation can support evolutionary inference. Approximations adequate for stand-level light interception can mislead for competition and selection among individuals.
